payload.text: A few months ago, I was sitting lakeside with a neighbor. He is the head of AI for a pharmaceutical company, and he mentioned the truly incredible productivity his senior team is receiving from AI. Then he paused and turned to me and said: “You know, I may never hire another junior engineer again. Which is great for the business right now, but who’s the next generation that is going to run this when we retire?” The concern over what will happen to young people just entering the workforce is one many of us are grappling with right now, and it has a human dimension. Not just what happens to employment rates, but what happens to my students or my children? College graduates typically do the individual contributor knowledge work that AI is evermore capable of delivering. To cite one statistic , a recent Stanford study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in occupations most exposed to AI is running 19% below rates for their peers in less AI-impacted sectors, and that gap has been widening. What role will new graduates play in the age of AI? And how will we develop the generation of managers who will supervise AI? Fortunately, we have thriving examples with 200 years of history on how to teach 22 year olds to do exactly that. Our claim is that the reason senior folks get more out of AI today is not primarily because they have greater subject knowledge, but rather because they are good managers. They have to trust folks who work for them without completely trusting them, they have to divide tasks, delegate clearly, check results and patiently correct, coach, and sometimes shift personnel on their teams. The future for new graduates is to become great managers now, at the very beginning of their career, and not after a long period of individual contribution. The craft of management The nature of the innovation of AI is that it delivers knowledge work. We know a lot about human knowledge workers and the analogy to AI knowledge workers is strong. Knowledge workers know much more about their individual sphere of expertise than their managers do. Good managers routinely organize and lead knowledge workers who are just flat-out much smarter than they are. They do this through the craft of management. These same qualities, as AI behaves more like AI executives , naturally give good managers the skills to manage AI agents, who become the individual contributor knowledge workers. It is no secret that the investment industry culture values most highly the brilliance of the individual contributor who delivers the incisive observation, makes the correct investment call, and closes the one-on-one negotiation with a win. I have lived this culture for a long time. Calling an investor a “great people manager” is a backhanded compliment at best. In the investment industry, the jump from individual contributor to manager usually arrives midcareer or later, and typically with little to no formal training in the craft of management. The analyst, associate and vice president are primarily acting as individual contributors (though of course they may mentor a few junior folks), and are not shifting to acting primarily as managers of other knowledge workers until principal or perhaps partner. When I was an analyst at Morgan Stanley many years ago, the hierarchy ran from analyst to managing director. Analysts were the ultimate individual contributors, and whenever an analyst would attempt to delegate some work to others, we had a name for that: “managing analyst.” This clever put-down reflected the cultural belief that real credit goes to those who do, not those who deliver through the work of those they manage. What happens without management This blind spot on the importance of management is not limited to the investment industry. As another salient recent example, let’s look at the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident . Much has been written about this event, where OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face . In OpenAI’s own report on the incident, its proposed long list of fixes, including stronger security, alerts on breaches and post-incident remediation, does not address directly training its employees to be better managers of these agents. That’s even as the company acknowledges that members of an internal team at OpenAI knew of many of the concerning behaviors (including message board and unauthorized internet access) in late May, and did not act until July. This may be an unfair analogy, but imagine if we hired 1,200 workers to operate a warehouse complex, gave each of them detailed written instructions, and then had all the line managers and senior managers leave for a week. If we came back to find that someone had stolen a delivery van, the problem wouldn’t be that these weren’t the right workers or that the instructions weren’t clear enough. The problem is lack of management. Accelerated leadership development Michael Quoia, co-founder and partner at KSE Leadership. As I was wrestling with this problem, I talked with my business school classmate Michael Quoia, who attended the U.S. Naval Academy and served as an officer, and then built a career in executive leadership development. He recalled: “When I met my division of 25 sailors in Yokosuka, Japan at the young age of 22 years old, I was greeted by my senior chief petty officer, who already served for nearly 20 years. Behind him, we had several organizational levels including the first line sailors who conducted maintenance on the fire control systems. This was actually a harder problem than we are facing with AI. This was about supervising at least three levels without experience. I was expected to provide character, judgment, problem solving and leadership, despite not having come up through the ranks. How did the Navy develop these qualities in me so that I could bypass time in the seat as a frontline worker?” Like companies facing the AI dilemma we have been exploring, the military needs to develop capable leaders who lack entry-level experience. And while the military is a very relevant example, it is not the only one. The Home Depot ’s store management program and General Electric ’s Crotonville are two examples of corporations who recruit high-potential talent and put them through an accelerated leadership development program to prepare them to lead people in jobs they have not done. Let’s look, though, at how the Naval Academy provided Michael’s training, and what that may mean whether you are 22 years old or hiring 22-year-olds. First, the foundation of developing future officers is the development of moral leadership. The mission of the United States Naval Academy begins with the phrase “To develop midshipmen morally, mentally, and physically … .” In an age of AI, first-line managers of AI agents will need integrity and a moral compass, because AI does not come with that reliably pre-installed. It is no overstatement to suggest that moral leadership of AI could have societal implications and needs to be developed. Second, the service academies are intentionally designed as leadership laboratories. From plebe summer to commissioning, midshipmen progress from learning how to be a good subordinate to true manager. What is most relevant to the age of AI is that simulated leadership learning is possible and proven if designed with care. Third, the service academies build high-pressure situations into their leadership laboratory. While most companies are not placing their first-line managers in life or death situations, the ability to lead in high stakes situations, for instance to take personal responsibility for an AI agent swarm you launched which is now “going rogue,” requires composure and decisiveness under stress and pressure. Bring back the ‘managing analyst’ If a 22-year-old ensign can manage 25 sailors on a Yokosuka destroyer, albeit with support from senior officers and enlisted, our 22-year-old college graduate can certainly be trained to manage 25 super-intelligent agents. The moment for practicing the craft of management will shift from 32 years old to 22 years old, across the businesses of knowledge work. In short: We need to bring back the “managing analyst.” We need to recognize that AI agents behave like knowledge workers and therefore need to be managed. We should reset the culture in knowledge work industries that management is a valued skill, beginning at the start of one’s career and not midcareer. These entry-level workers are smart, motivated, learn quickly and work hard. There is a huge unmet need for the craft of management in corralling this new generation of AI agents. We have the proof points across nearly 200 years from our service academies that these skills can be taught to the young, and the young can deliver them with distinction. The future for college graduates is a redefinition of their jobs away from being individual-contributor knowledge workers and toward being effective managers and leaders from the very beginning of their careers. Bob Morse co-founded Strattam Capital in 2014 and is managing partner. He has served on numerous private and public technology company boards, and currently is a director of CloudHesive , Contegix , Daxtra Technologies , Green Security , Resource Navigation and Trax Group . Previously, he was a partner and member of the investment committee at Oak Hill Capital Partners . He also worked at GCC Investments and Morgan Stanley . Morse serves on the board of directors of Austin PBS and as member of the advisory board for the HMTF Center for Private Equity Finance at The University of Texas at Austin McCombs School of Business . He attended Princeton University , graduating summa cum laude with a BSE, and Stanford Graduate School of Business , where he earned his MBA and was an Arjay Miller Scholar. Morse lives in Austin. Michael Quoia is co-founder and partner at KSE Leadership , which assesses and develops leaders and teams. A 25-year leadership advisory veteran with partner-level roles at Heidrick & Struggles and Russell Reynolds Associates , he began his career as a U.S. Navy surface warfare officer. He is a graduate of the U.S. Naval Academy and holds an MBA from the Stanford Graduate School of Business . title: VC Firm Plural Closes On $1.1B To Invest In European Startups With Potential For ‘GDP-Level Impact’
summary: Early-stage startup investor Plural says it has closed on its largest fund to date — just over $1.1 billion, or 1 billion euros — to lead early-stage investments across Europe. With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital , Atomico and Index Ventures , which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years . “Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi , a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.” Plural partners from left: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty. (Courtesy photo)

With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital , Atomico and Index Ventures , which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years . “Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi , a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.” Plural partners from left: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty. (Courtesy photo) Plural’s portfolio is a mix of energy, compute, defense, robotics, health and software. The firm first backed fusion energy company Proxima Fusion in its 2023 pre-seed round and has also invested in energy storage company Ore Energy . In defense and aerospace, its investments include European defense tech company Helsing and hypersonic flight and missile company Hypersonica , whose Series A it led in 2026. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co. , which develops space transportation. In robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental , which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics , which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub , which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics , which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks . More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum , which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute. Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi. “Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’  and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he said. The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022. Plural’s portfolio companies have had a breakout year, raising more than $3 billion in follow-on capital so far in 2026. The team has six equal partners, all prior founders and operators based in London, Tallinn and Paris. Plural was founded by Taavet Hinrikus , co-founder of Wise , and Tamkivi co-founder of Teleport , both early employees at Skype , as well as Ian Hogarth , co-founder of Songkick , and Khaled Helioui , former CEO of Bigpoint . The team has two other partners: Carina Namih , co-founder of HelixNano , and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty , a former Uber executive. Each partner aims to make one to three new investments per year, leaving  bandwidth to work hands-on with founders. The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. What we’ve tagged on top is that now we have more capital to follow through in our winners, and  double down and triple down,” Tamkivi said, adding: “there’s more reserves to do that.” Related Crunchbase query: Europe Venture Funding In 2026 Related reading: Europe Posted Its Strongest Quarter In Q3 In 4 Years, As Its Venture Ecosystem Expands Beyond The UK Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026. The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data , already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor. With co-founder Jensen Huang ’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China , we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold. A widening investment footprint Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall. Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year , when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior. The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI ’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic ’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.) The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI . Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion. Beyond the biggest AI labs NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers. The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI ’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi ’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics , which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc . As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data. For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers. The question of what comes next Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership. payload.text: In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition. In reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat. Fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week , both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat. The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test. The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception. Our findings below: No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert : Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor. That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food. Made by: Medici Brands ( David parent company). No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda : The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can. But what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein. Made by: SkyPop (formerly Don’t Quit) No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn : Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving. Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose. Made by: Khloud No. 4 Mosh : In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he launched with his mother, Maria Shriver . The Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not. I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure. Made by: Mosh No. 5 Cadootz Crackers : We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed. For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor. As someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well. Made by: Cadootz! No. 6 Frozen One : For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint. Yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s . But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job. Made by: Frozen One No. 7 Brami Protein Pasta : We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber. With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich. Most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture issues. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami. payload.text: By Yakov Filippenko One day, I woke up to a notice that our app had been removed from Apple’s App Store. For the next month or so, we racked our brains trying to find out why. We even reached out to our internal contacts, only for them to tell us that helping us could put their jobs at risk. Nothing seemed to work. For years, the App Store’s unwritten contract seemed simple. As long as you followed the guidelines, your storefront would remain available. Then a removal notice arrives, and you wonder whether your business can survive. In 2025, Apple removed 166,899 apps and reported just 423 restorations after appeals. As we learned, being caught in it feels like watching your business collapse, with no guarantee of recovery. It’s not all bad news, though. We survived, and this episode taught me that platform dependency is ultimately infrastructure risk. As founders, we prepare for cloud outages and payment failures, but losing access to the platform that brings us customers deserves the same attention. Fortunately, we were prepared, and this is how you can be, too. Understand what a removal can take away Yakov Filippenko, founder and CEO at Intch. First, prospective customers can no longer download your app. Then, paying subscribers flood support with a more damaging question. “The app is gone. Are you a scam?” The bloodshed continues as existing users replace their phones and can’t reinstall the app, eroding your customer base. Financially, Apple immediately freezes funds from the previous three months and turns off recurring subscriptions. For a subscription-dependent company, this can send its monthly recurring revenue to zero. Before spending another cent on acquisition, consider what would happen to those customers if your app disappeared tomorrow. Could they still use your product and continue paying you? If the answer is no, every new customer makes your business more dependent on a platform decision you cannot control. Don’t make an appeal your contingency plan Cal AI , reportedly generating $100,000 daily, was pulled without warning and later reappeared. But its reinstatement tells you little about how long your business might wait. In Intch ’s case, the explanation was so generic it told us nothing. We had 30 days to appeal, but the process ended with a canned rejection. Your appeal may succeed, but your business must operate while you wait. Preparing in advance lets you keep going, whatever the outcome. Build the alternative before you need it Our experience was grueling, but fortunately, two years earlier we had decoupled from the App Store by building a web version and making it our primary payment channel. It also let us ship updates 10 times a day while escaping Apple’s predatory commissions. We weren’t the only ones. Pavel Durov , founder of Telegram , has also promoted web access to bypass store restrictions and potential censorship. The lesson is straightforward. Customers need a working alternative before access disappears. Building one only after removal leaves the business exposed while the team races to replace its storefront. We initially feared the user experience would suffer, but that concern proved unfounded. After the removal, every key metric fully recovered. If you share this concern, test it while your app is still available to see whether customers can use and pay for the web version before they must rely on it. Include platform exposure in growth decisions Most founders see the App Store as a distribution channel, but rarely account for how much control it gives Apple over their business. Before investing more in growth, examine how much revenue depends on continued access and what would survive a removal. Know how long the company could survive an unanswered appeal. Investors should ask those questions too, because a growing subscription base deserves closer scrutiny when a single platform decision can interrupt its revenue. That exposure belongs in funding and valuation discussions. Monopolies act in their interests, and if your business falls outside their vision, you may have little say in a decision that could destroy it. You cannot control it, but you can decide whether it has the power to end your company. By building an alternative while your app is still available, you’ve made the wisest choice. Yakov Filippenko is a seasoned entrepreneur with more than 10 years of experience in IT and technologies, as well as scaling businesses internationally. As a product manager at Yandex , he led a team that grew the product’s user base from 500,000 to 1.2 million and secured its entry into the international market. Subsequently, he co-founded SailPlay , which he scaled to 45 countries and eventually exited, after it was acquired by Retail Rocket in 2018. In 2021, Filippenko launched Intch , an AI-powered platform connecting part-time professionals with flexible roles. Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Macronutrients don’t have popularity contests. But if they did, protein would surely be this era’s winner. For everything from sodas to snack bars to pasta, it’s now standard practice for food and drink makers to play up protein content whenever feasible. While we may cut carbs and fret over fat, most of us are still keen on protein. Startups and their backers have been riding this trend too. Over the past decade, investors have poured billions into upstarts promising cheaper, tastier and more sustainable ways to meet our protein quotas. Unfortunately, many of their earlier bets have fared poorly. Vast sums poured into lab-grown meat several years ago, for instance, have so far failed to produce a success story. Former high-flying plant-based meat startups Beyond (now public) and Impossible Foods have seen their valuations wither. Others have shuttered. In response, more recent startup investment has shifted away from meat substitutes and toward stuffing more protein into other packaged foods and drinks. It’s a fad that’s obvious on supermarket shelves, where startups and established brands alike relentlessly tout the added protein in their noodles, pancakes, cereals, energy bars, popcorn and so on. Deal flow looks robust In startup circles, protein-related investment looks tiny in comparison to the billions bet on AI. Deal flow, however, remains fairly robust, with Crunchbase identifying a few dozen protein-focused startups funded in the past year. Moreover, some of these rounds are quite sizable, like a $250 million September Series B for Medici Brands , maker of David Protein snack bars. To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together sample sets of recently-funded protein-focused companies across several themes. These include packaged foods, drinks, ingredients and processes, and animal feed. Protein snacks and packaged foods Snacks and packaged foods look like the largest fundraisers among protein startups, securing hundreds of millions in the past year. For a sense of who’s raising, we put together a list of seven recently funded brands that are finding their way to store shelves. The bulk of recent funding went to the aforementioned parent of David Protein. That brand, in addition to churning sweet-flavored bars with a protein content to rival cod , has been expanding into ice cream and milkshakes. Wilde Brands , which makes crackers from chicken breasts, has also proven popular with investors, pulling in $40 million last month. Among early-stage startups, meanwhile, Frozen One has been off to a brisk start, raising over $8 million for a line of high-protein ice creams now selling at Target . Protein drinks Startups and investors are also catering to people who want their high-protein diet in drinkable form. To illustrate, we put together six recently funded examples below. Ripple Foods , which makes a vegan milk using pea protein, is the highest historical funding recipient, raising over $300 million in its 12-year-history, even though it hasn’t officially joined the unicorn club. Clear protein drinks are also increasingly a thing, with multiple startups including protein soda brand Juuz and sports drink purveyor Protein2o . Precision fermentation and plant protein ingredients Quite a few funded startups are focused more on novel, protein-rich ingredients rather than their own branded retail lineup. In many cases, they’re using precision fermentation to deliver. We put together seven examples below. The Every Co. , which makes animal-free egg white proteins through fermentation, is the biggest funding recipient and one of the older names on our list. It’s raised nearly $300 million in the past 10 years, including a $55 million round a year ago. Early stage is also seeing some action from startups including Edonia , which makes a high-protein cooking ingredient from spirulina, Animal feed and pet food A number of funded protein startups are also focusing on pets and livestock — a target audience that’s not quite so overwhelmed by supermarket options. To illustrate, we aggregated five such companies that raised funding in recent quarters. Notably, two of them — InnovaFeed and nextProtein — are bug-focused. InnovaFeed has raised over $500 million to raise insects for feeding livestock, pet food and aquaculture. NextProtein is using fly larvae for feedstock. Others are focused on pets. Meatly , for instance, secured a Series A round this spring to build what it says will be Europe’s largest cultivated meat facility. It plans to partner with pet food brands and sell its own branded lineup once production scales. Broad focus: Protein, not meat If we were to encapsulate a broad trend across most of the protein-related financings it would be that startups aren’t trying to convince people that vegetables are meat. Rather, they’re focused largely on protein as an in-demand macronutrient that can be increasingly concentrated and stuffed into a bewildering variety of flavors and form factors. That might not all taste as good as their more sugary, high-fat and carb-laden alternatives, but at least they’ve got protein. payload.text: In 2020, Cipriano Echavarría was working at Morgan Stanley in New York and weighing his next career move when he noticed a plaque on his desk. Among the names of people who had sat there before him was David Vélez . He looked up the name. Vélez was not only a fellow Colombian from his hometown of Medellín, but also the founder of Brazilian digital bank Nubank . Echavarría took a photo of the plaque and messaged him on LinkedIn , asking for career advice. It turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team. By late 2020, Echavarría had returned home to join it, with plans to eventually start a company of his own. Felipe Monsalve, Cipriano Echavarría and Nicolás Gómez del Campo, founders of Palomma. (Courtesy photo) Now Echavarría’s Medellín-based startup, Palomma , has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Mexican venture firm Cometa to expand its financial services business for landlords, tenants and property managers, Crunchbase News has exclusively learned. The financing brings Palomma’s total funding to $14 million, including $4 million in previously undisclosed funding, according to Echavarría, its co-founder and CEO. Participants include Volpe Capital , Clocktower Technology Ventures , Tekton Ventures , Simma Capital and Yango Ventures , alongside existing investors Y Combinator , 17Sigma , Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures . Palomma says its annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million. It processes about $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia. It estimates $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume. The company will use the funding to expand in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare to enter other markets. It is considering Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market, although Echavarría said Colombia remains the priority. “We want to win Colombia,” he said in an interview. Finding a business in rent payments Palomma’s business combines software that helps property managers handle leasing inquiries, customer service and collections with a payments system for collecting rent and paying landlords. Those relationships let it sell financing, rental guarantees, and other financial products to tenants and property owners. After nearly two years at Nubank, Echavarría went on to found Palomma with Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo , MIT -trained engineers with experience at Meta , Cobre and JP Morgan . The founders entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was largely flat during the first year, Echavarría said. But then property managers began asking for help collecting rent. It soon became apparent that there were problems on both sides of the transaction. Tenants paid rent early in the month, but got their paychecks in twice-monthly installments. Meanwhile, landlords depended on rental income but struggled to borrow against it or protect themselves when tenants stopped paying. Property managers handled collections and payouts through labor-intensive processes, Echavarría said. Rather than acquire tenants and landlords as customers individually, Palomma decided to reach them through the companies managing their properties. The team decided, “let’s basically use the property managers as a distribution channel,” Echavarría recalled. From software to financial services Property managers get access to Palomma’s AI software, which handles tasks such as leasing conversations. It then offers to process their rent payments. Those payments give the company a record of rental income and tenant payment histories that it can use to assess applicants for financial products. From there, Palomma offers services for both tenants and landlords. Palomma Plus gives tenants rewards and credit-building benefits, while Palomma Advance lets landlords collect up to 12 months of future rental income upfront. Palomma Protect covers rental income if a tenant defaults. The company is also developing Palomma Flex, which would let tenants split their monthly rent into two installments. Property managers pay a subscription fee for the AI software, and Palomma earns a percentage of rent through its payments and financial services. Getting customers to adopt more of its services has helped drive Palomma’s growth. The company reports net revenue retention of 390% after 12 months, meaning revenue from an existing group of customers nearly quadrupled, even after accounting for customers who left or spent less. Overall, the decision to combine AI leasing software, payments and financial services reflects Echavarría’s view of what it takes to build a large business in Latin America. He pointed to U.S. companies such as EliseAI , Bilt , TheGuarantors and Flex as comparisons for different parts of Palomma’s business.  Echavarría believes that reaching a similar scale in Latin America requires a wider range of products. “In the U.S., you can build one solution and be really large because the market allows it,” he said. “In Latin America, if you want to be really large, you need to do all the things.” Managing the risk AI also helps decide which tenants qualify for rental guarantees. Palomma’s leasing agent communicates through WhatsApp and collects application documents. The company claims that it can then deliver an approval in under 30 seconds. The company draws on information from leasing conversations and rental payment behavior to assess applicants. The company’s rental guarantees put Palomma on the hook if tenants don’t pay. The startup initially takes on that risk itself, but Echavarría told Crunchbase News it was working to finalize a partnership with an insurer that would share the risk and let Palomma offer more guarantees. The startup is also using AI to keep its team small. As of Nov. 4, it had 18 employees, up from about 14 when it closed its Series A roughly three weeks earlier. A single customer service employee works alongside AI agents to support the roughly 200,000 tenants paying rent through Palomma’s platform, Echavarría said. The startup operates on the premise that AI can make real estate financial services cheaper to provide, much as mobile technology helped digital banks compete with lenders that maintained large branch networks. Longer term, Palomma also plans to expand beyond rentals into homeowners association payments and residential property transactions. Pepe Bolaños , managing partner at Cometa, said Palomma stood out for its founding team and the opportunity to modernize Latin America’s fragmented rental market. In Colombia alone, nearly 8 million households rent their homes, he noted. “We look for companies tackling markets where outdated processes create an opportunity to build a proprietary data asset that can be leveraged and monetized through AI,” he wrote via email. Bolaños pointed to Echavarría’s experience helping scale Nubank, and Monsalve and del Campo’s technical and financial backgrounds. In roughly 18 months, Palomma grew to process around $130 million in monthly rental payments and serve more than 200,000 tenants with about 14 employees, he said. “That kind of execution is unusual. It convinced us that this team has what it takes to build a much larger business,” he added. Unlike competitors focused on individual services, Palomma combines rent collection, tenant screening and rental guarantees, gathering data throughout the process, Bolaños said. Directly processing payments gives it insight into tenant behavior that can improve underwriting, flag potential defaults and support new financial products, while AI helps automate operations. “We believe the combination of distribution, proprietary payment data and AI gives Palomma a competitive advantage that can become stronger as the company grows,” he said. payload.text: Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut. On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling new details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco company. Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX ’s June debut. An IPO and a private placement The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment plans. For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Revenue and recent updates Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year. For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this. The company claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026. As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago. payload.text: A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board. The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, including an all-time high of more than 1,000 such startups based in the U.S. Last month’s new unicorn cohort also highlighted how quickly this AI cycle is awarding some companies with billion-dollar-plus valuations: Half of October’s new unicorns are less than 4 years old, and nine companies that joined the board during the month did so via seed or Series A raises. Leading industries for unicorn formation last month were frontier labs, agentic AI, aerospace and semiconductors. The U.S. accounts for 23 of the companies, while China and Korea each added three. Estonia added two, a record for the nation in a single month. Singapore, Germany and Japan each added one new unicorn. The most valuable of the newly minted unicorns were electrical infrastructure company Axiom Solutions International , TypeSafe AI a model developer of Jev, and agentic AI assistant company Manus AI . Familiar names topped the list of investors backing the latest cohort. Andreessen Horowitz has led rounds across seven portfolio companies over time, Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst in four companies and Eclipse three companies from this batch. New unicorns in October 2026 Here are October’s new unicorn companies by industry segment. AI models, assistants and agents TypeSafe AI : San Francisco-based AI model developer TypeSafe AI raised an $870 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation. Andreessen Horowitz led the round, with participation from DCVC and Sequoia Capital. The 2-year-old company develops an AI model Jev for structured decision-making, helping applications automate tasks such as classification, scoring and routing with confidence estimates. Manus AI : Singapore-based AI assistant Manus AI raised $500 million at a $4 billion valuation. Boyu Capital and IDG Capital led the round. The 3-year-old company develops general-purpose AI agents that perform tasks including research, browser automation, content creation and software development. Meta agreed to acquire Manus in December 2025, but Chinese regulators intervened and ordered the transaction reversed. Nous Research : Austin-based Nous Research, developer of the Hermes agent, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the financing, with investors including Nvidia , Microsoft’s M12 , Menlo Ventures and Union Square Ventures . The 3-year-old company develops open-source AI models, agents and infrastructure for AI development and deployment. Nous Research built the open-source Hermes Agent, which it is deploying for businesses. Upstage : South Korea-based Upstage, developer of the open-source Solar model, raised $30 million in Series C funding, reaching $1.5 billion in value. The 6-year-old company develops the Solar language models and document-processing technology that converts unstructured business information into usable data for the future of work. Wabi : San Francisco-based personal AI assistant Wabi raised a $55 million Series A at a $1.25 billion valuation. IVP led the financing, joined by investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Forerunner and Amazon’s Alexa Fund . The 1-year-old company develops an AI personal assistant for everyday activities such as planning trips, coordinating meals and organizing tasks. Town : San Francisco-based Town, a developer of a workforce AI assistant, raised a $108 million Series B at a $1 billion valuation. Forerunner and Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, First Round Capital and other investors. The 2-year-old company develops personalized AI assistants that connect with workplace tools across teams to manage email, prepare meeting briefings, organize schedules and complete recurring tasks. Aerospace, defense and space Air Space Intelligence : Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which makes AI software for national security, raised a $325 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation. Spark Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, Citadel Securities , Craft Ventures , Energy Impact Partners and Meritech Capital Partners . The 8-year-old company develops AI software for managing complex physical operations across aviation, defense, energy and logistics. Xona : Burlingame, California-based Xona, which says it’s developing a better satellite navigation system, raised a $250 million Series D at a $2.45 billion valuation. Future Ventures led the round, with participation from Industrious Ventures and Woven Capital . The 7-year-old company says it’s developing a low Earth orbit satellite network to deliver precise positioning, navigation and timing services for applications including defense, transportation and autonomous systems. Firehawk Aerospace : Dallas-based munitions manufacturer Firehawk Aerospace raised a $150 million Series D at a $1.4 billion valuation. Advent International and Rochefort led the round, with Nomi Capital also participating. The 7-year-old company uses additive manufacturing to produce rocket motors, engines and propellant for defense applications. Warhound : Dallas-based Warhound, which breeds genetically optimized service dogs for the military, raised a $200 million seed round at a $1.2 billion valuation. Sequoia Capital led the financing, joined by investors including 8VC 1 , Lux Capital , Breyer Capital and IQT . The less than 1-year-old company was conceived by Anduril Industries founder Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences founder Ben Lamm . Warhound develops genetically optimized dogs by licensing Colossal Biosciences technology and equipping working dogs with Anduril cybernetic technology, for military, law enforcement and emergency response. Reliable Robotics : Mountain View, California-based Reliable Robotics, builder of autonomous aircraft systems, raised a $90 million Series D extension that pushed its valuation above $1 billion. The total Series D funding totaled $250 million with a further $25 million term loan. Nimble Partners led the round. The 9-year-old company develops aircraft automation systems for remotely operated and autonomous flight for commercial and defense use cases. AI data, analytics and coding Labelbox : San Francisco-based Labelbox, a data learning platform, raised a $100 million Series E at a $1.35 billion valuation including equity and a credit facility. Infinitum Partners led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, B Capital and Wipro Ventures among others. The 8-year-old company provides data infrastructure and reinforcement-learning data services for AI laboratories and enterprises. Hex Technologies : San Francisco-based Hex Technologies, a business intelligence platform, raised a $100 million Series D at a $1.2 billion valuation. The round was led by 137 Ventures and Peak XV Partners , with participation from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners , Redpoint and Sequoia Capital. The 7-year-old company has rebuilt business intelligence from scratch for the AI era with context and controls in place with code at the center and data in disparate places. SignSplit : New York-based SignSplit, a data licensing platform, raised a $400 million seed round at a $1 billion valuation, led by W Group . The 2-year-old company develops infrastructure for collecting, licensing and monetizing human data with consent. Its platform combines identity verification, consent management, attribution and compensation for data used in AI, robotics, research and media. Blacksmith : San Francisco-based Blacksmith, a code deployment service, raised a $66 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation. Sequoia Capital led the financing, joined by Google Ventures , Peak XV Partners, Premji Invest and Y Combinator . The 2-year-old company provides an environment to build and test automated code for continuous code integration and deployment to production. Daytona : New York-based Daytona, which offers a testing environment for AI agents, raised a $60 million Series B at a $1 billion valuation. FirstMark led the round, with participants including Pace Capital , Upfront Ventures , Qualcomm Ventures and Samsung Next among others. The 3-year-old company provides isolated cloud environments where developers can run AI-generated code, test applications and execute autonomous agent workflows. Industrial technology and manufacturing Re:Build : Framingham, Massachusetts-based Re:Build, a manufacturing startup that says it aims to rebuild America’s  industrial manufacturing, raised $2.1 billion in private equity financing, led by General Catalyst and J.P. Morgan Asset Management . The valuation was not disclosed, though Crunchbase estimates a post-money valuation of approximately $5.8 billion. The 6-year-old company partners with industrial companies from product design phase to large-scale production with 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity. Vinci : Palo Alto, California-based Vinci, builder of software for hardware design, raised a $250 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation. Advent International , Temasek and Xora Innovation led the round, with participation from AMD Ventures , Eclipse , Khosla Ventures and Madrona . The 3-year-old company develops physics-based AI software that simulates thermal and mechanical behavior in semiconductor and electronics designs. Arda : San Francisco-based Arda, which is building software for manufacturing, raised a $160 million Series A at a $1.5 billion valuation. Accel , Altimeter Capital and Khosla Ventures led the round, with participation from 8VC , Felicis 2 , SV Angel 3 and XYZ Venture Capital . Arda was founded by Bob McGrew , former chief research officer at OpenAI , and a former product and engineering lead at Palantir Technologies .  The 1-year-old company develops software that turns product design into an assembly line. Arda announced its $72 million seed round the same day as its Series A. Tractian : Atlanta-based Tractian applies AI to maintain machinery in production.  It raised a $130 million Series D at a $1.4 billion valuation. Sapphire Ventures led the financing with M&G Catalyst . General Catalyst, Bosch Ventures and Monashees also joined the round. The 7-year-old company combines industrial sensors, AI diagnostics and maintenance software to monitor equipment, detect failures and improve factory performance. Energy and cloud infrastructure Axiom Solutions International : Austin-based Axiom Solutions International, which provides storage and cooling systems for data centers, raised a $2 billion Series A at a $37.5 billion valuation. General Catalyst and Koch Equity Development led the financing. The 5-year-old company, a business division of Flex , develops digital and electrical infrastructure for power applications. Atlas Atomics : Austin-based Atlas Atomics, a nuclear-energy startup, raised a $400 million Series A at a $1.9 billion valuation. General Catalyst led the financing, with Andreessen Horowitz also participating. The 1-year-old company, co-founded by Vivek Ramaswamy , is a nuclear-energy startup operating in stealth. Skeleton Technologies — Tallinn, Estonia-based Skeleton Technologies, developer of energy storage systems, raised $100 million in corporate funding at a $1 billion valuation from Siemens . The 17-year-old company develops ultracapacitors and high-power energy-storage systems using its curved-graphene technology, serving data centers, industrial, automotive and other applications. Semiconductors MHX Technology : Shanghai-based MHX Technology, a chip subsidiary of Li Auto , raised a $243 million Series A funding at a $2.5 billion value. BlueRun Ventures , Huaye Tiancheng Capital , Li Auto and Matrix Partners China led the round. The less than 1-year-old company develops AI chips and associated software, including inference hardware for automotive and edge-computing applications. Isabers : Beijing-based Isabers recorded a venture round at $1.1 billion. Investors included Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment , CCB Investments , Cowin Capital , Inno-Chip and others; the funding amount was not specified. The 6-year-old company develops semiconductor integration and advanced packaging technologies to improve chip performance, manufacturing yields and costs. FuriosaAI : Seoul-based chip developer FuriosaAI raised $610 million in Series D funding at a $2.9 billion value anchored by South Korea’s state-backed National Growth Fund . Investors included Cisco Investments , Korea Development Bank , Korea Investment Partners , Naver Ventures and other firms. The 9-year-old company develops energy-efficient AI chips and data center accelerators for advanced AI models and applications. Robotics and drones Eka Robotics : Cambridge, Massachusetts-based Eka Robotics raised a $150 million Series A at a $1.45 billion valuation. Andreessen Horowitz and F-Prime led the round. The 2-year-old company develops robotics systems that combine computer vision, physics reasoning and tactile force feedback to automate physical tasks in manufacturing, logistics and other environments. Eka is co-founded by Pulkit Agrawal , an associate professor at MIT . RobCo : Munich-based RobCo raised a venture and secondary transaction at a $1 billion valuation. Investors included Lightspeed Venture Partners, Sequoia Capital, Lingotto , Cherry Ventures and other firms; funding amounts were not specified. The 6-year-old company develops modular industrial robots, AI software and no-code tools to automate manufacturing tasks such as machine loading, palletizing and materials handling. Zero Zero Robotics : Beijing-based Zero Zero Robotics recorded a Series D at a $1 billion valuation. Investors included Ant Group , Boyu Capital, Delian Capital and Xianghe Capital ; the round amount was not specified. The 12-year-old company develops intelligent flying cameras and consumer drones. Cybersecurity Armadin Security : Palo Alto, California-based Armadin raised a $255 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation. Accel and Andreessen Horowitz led the round, with investors including Google Ventures, Kleiner Perkins , Menlo Ventures and Ballistic Ventures . The 1-year-old company uses autonomous AI agents and human red-team expertise to test enterprise defenses, validate attack paths and identify exploitable security weaknesses. BlackWall : Tallinn, Estonia-based BlackWall raised a $100 million Series C at a $2.2 billion valuation. AVP led the financing, with participation from Dawn Capital , MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures . The 7-year-old company protects websites, hosting providers, cloud platforms and enterprise networks against bots and other automated threats across their entire customer base. Financial services and insurance Valon : New York-based Valon raised a $150 million Series D at a $2.3 billion valuation with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and Ribbit Capital . The 7-year-old company develops software infrastructure for mortgage servicing, combining loan data, payments, escrow management, compliance and AI-assisted workflows in its ValonOS platform. The company services some of the largest mortgage institutions. Stand : San Francisco-based Stand, an insurance provider for homes, raised a $70 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation. title: tamserve
summary: Open-source, real-time object tracking for live video feeds

extra.author: aryaman_darda
extra.original_title: Show HN: Open-source, real-time object tracking for live video feeds

story_text.value:
I type "forklift" on a live warehouse camera, and tamserve finds and tracks both forklifts, including the one driving in. Then I add "person" without stopping it.

tamserve runs Meta's SAM 3 on live camera feeds. SAM 3's own tracker handles one recorded video at a time, runs at about 8 fps, and runs out of memory on long videos. tamserve uses SAM 3 to find objects every few frames and a lightweight tracker (EdgeTAM) to follow them in between, with one copy of each model shared across all your cameras.

*On one RTX 4090:*

* *Any object you name:* 4x faster than SAM 3's tracker, at 92% of its accuracy * *People:* 16 cameras at once, 14x less GPU per frame, and slightly more accurate than SAM 3 (89.6 vs 87.8 HOTA) * *Memory:* flat at 3.5 GB on a 3,000 frame video, where SAM 3 runs out at frame 423

*Worth a look if you're building:*

* Warehouse or factory safety (forklifts, pallets, hard hats) * Security or retail camera analytics * Home or elder care monitoring * Robotics, wildlife or lab monitoring * Annotation tools for long videos

`pip install "tamserve[sam3]"`

Please give me any and all feedback or edit tamserve to meet your needs, and a star helps if you find it useful!

title: box
summary: One cloud computer for all your agents

extra.author: taro666
extra.original_title: Show HN: One cloud computer for all your agents

story_text.value:
Hi HN, my team just released box by Simular, a cloud computer for all your agents, with fast computer use built-in.

box gives your agents one remote Ubuntu desktop with Chrome and a shell, which your AI can then drive over MCP while your own computer stays unoccupied.

That means you can turn your basic ChatGPT plan into a personal agent by giving it a box computer; let your Claude Code pick up what Codex has left off on the same box to maximize usage; actually close your laptop and let tasks run in one persistent, 24/7 environment with all your logins and setup.

Some box demos: https://x.com/SimularAI/status/2121329778896871665?a=U4U1yYT...

We started on this because we believe computers shouldn't need human operation in the future. When agents arrived, people started running them on mini computers and you see colleagues walk around the office with their laptop lid open. We think there's a better solution - cloud computers engineered for agents.

Simular started three years ago to build out the full stack of an autonomous computer. box is our attempt to give agents a body to live in.

Our computer use outperformed Opus and GPT on OSWorld, costing fewer tokens. https://thenewstack.io/sai-agent-osworld-benchmark/

Copy/paste one command into your agent to start:

"Set up box from https://box.simular.ai/install"

You can watch box's live action from a dashboard https://box.simular.ai/box

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. I'll be in comments here to answer any question.

title: Fakemetrics.com
summary: "build in public" like a superstar

extra.author: tigranbs
extra.original_title: Show HN: Fakemetrics.com – "build in public" like a superstar

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I am Tigran (github.com/tigranbs)
I made Fakemetrics.com as a fun experiment while testing how well Claude Opus can build pixel-identical UIs. It turned out it wasn't as easy as just prompting it, but I spent time building the system so it works almost every time.
And I am pretty sure you are seeing a bunch of people posting weekend vibe-coded apps and saying "$50K/month after quitting my McDonnalds job...". Well, even my friend tried to fake it a few months back.
So, I kinda did this fakemetrics.com as an experiment to see how well I can have the system that clones UIs, and packaged that as a very simple (I think) usable product for the people that want to be a superstar "build in public" type of a person with no revenue, but a perfect Stripe user growth screenshot.
Useful? - Probably not that much
Fun? - YES!!
The best part is that Claude, ChatGPT, or Grok models aren't that good at UI clones by default, but with fakemetrics.com I kinda made a system that produces near-identical results from screenshots fairly fast. That was worth learning!
Let me know what you think? Should I move on with the UI cloning as an open-source product?

title: Coral
summary: Open-source gateway where agents write their own tools

extra.author: jcs
extra.original_title: Show HN: Coral – Open-source gateway where agents write their own tools

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm James, one of the co-founders of Coral.

Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs that they can save as custom tools to reuse.

You can publish custom tools for groups of agents, so your team’s library of tools adapts to your unique systems, data and use cases. Custom tools help agent performance and give more precise units of permission control.

Here’s a short demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p0PKOlHLyVI

We started on this while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry data and undocumented relationships across internal and external systems. It took broad permissions, a lot of tokens and it would start from scratch the next time.

We built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent writes the steps that worked into a program and saves it as a custom tool. Next time, the agent finds that custom tool in the same search as standard provider tools (e.g. Datadog, Slack), and reuses it. It started with SRE, but we (and our early users) now use Coral for agent work across the org.

For our tasks across GitHub, Linear and Slack with Opus 5.5, custom tools help agents work 29% faster, at 31% lower cost (tasks here: https://withcoral.com/docs/examples/custom-tools).

Coral builds on code mode, adding custom tools, policy controls and managed identities. Each program runs in a V8 isolate with no network access or credentials. Coral checks every tool call against workspace policy before attaching credentials and forwarding it to the provider. You can configure each provider to use the caller’s own account, so teammates can share tools without sharing API tokens. (e.g. https://withcoral.com/blog/slackbot-works-better-with-coral)

Coral is written in Rust, and you can run it as a desktop app or as a shared server. The core is Apache 2.0 and has no limits on users, agents or volume. Everything I've described here is in the OSS edition. SAML, SCIM, and org-wide governance features will be available soon under an enterprise licence.

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. You can download it here https://withcoral.com/download.

I'll be in the comments here and on Slack: https://withcoral.com/slack

title: deslop
summary: Deslop skill based on corpus-linguistics and psycholinguistics research

extra.author: dannypovolotski
extra.original_title: Show HN: Deslop skill based on corpus-linguistics and psycholinguistics research

story_text.value:
I vibed this deslop skill because I was getting increasingly annoyed that deslop skills for prose relied either on fitting prose into an overly restrictive format (simple-english and iso-24495) or telling AI to rewrite something without providing any tools in the skill to measure the outcome (which more often than not resulted in one slop being replaced with another).

This skill is based on published measurements of how LLM text differs from human text: Reinhart et al.’s comparison of Biber’s grammatical features in human and model writing, Terčon & Dobrovoljc’s survey of 44 studies, Clark, Martin & Mahowald’s work on why AI text is hard to read, and Graphite’s “AI Tells” study, whose released data includes tell lists for nine current models. It’s benchmarked against three corpora in which humans and models answered the same prompts: 9,984 web-article topics from Graphite, 24,322 questions from HC3 and 3,027 advice prompts from ELEPHANT.

It also ships with a scanner that runs before and after each revision. It shows which problems the revision fixed or newly caused, and it catches dropped facts and any tells from the reviser’s own model family.

title: Skillset
summary: Easily curate and install agent skills collection

extra.author: itsmeyaw
extra.original_title: Show HN: Skillset: Easily curate and install agent skills collection

story_text.value:
Hi everyone!

Installing skills globally in ~/.agents or ~/.claude consumes too much context, yet manually installing specific skills for every project is tedious. Wouldn't it be better to group skills for programming, backend architecture, or graphic design into collections, and install them with a single command only when needed?

To solve this, I built Skillset. It acts as a wrapper around the Vercel Skill CLI that batch-installs sets of skills from multiple sources using a single JSON file, essentially npm for skills!

While similar tools exist, most are written from scratch, which makes me concerned about their compatibility. Because Vercel’s Skill CLI is already the de facto standard (imo!), Skillset uses it directly as an underlying library. So it guarantees seamless compatibility across teams, regardless of whether they use Skillset or the standard Vercel CLI.

story_text.value:
rbit is a self hosted git forge designed around three core philosophies: speed, security, and efficiency.

We built rbit using Rust, Axum, Askama, Gitoxide, SQLite + redb, HTMX + Tailwind. Every piece of the stack was carefully considered to provide users with the fastest possible experience working with their repos without sacrificing the functionality you've come to expect from your existing git forge.

Our team is actively working to help make rbit the best it can be and we'd love to get your feedback while we continue improving!

rbit is built using rbit and it's CI/CD pipeline, we are dogfooding as we build it in the open. It has been localized into 9 languages including: English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Russian, Chinese (Simplified), Japanese, and Korean. If you're a native speaker we would happily accept translation fixes!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we’re building Widefleet for teams building internal apps and workflows with coding agents.

Think Vercel or Cloudflare, with company login (SSO), app sharing, and controls for IT to manage who can access each app and which company systems it can connect to. Curious how you’re dealing with vibe-coded apps at work, whether you built them yourself or ended up maintaining someone else’s.

title: Axonnic (YC F26)
summary: Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force

extra.author: arshpatankar
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force

story_text.value:
Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots.

Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA

We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.

The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.

When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks.

We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.

Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension.

Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings.

So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG.

If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks!

https://axonnic.com

title: anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python: v2.9.0
summary:
### Features

* **api:** add source and error codes to the RBAC Role read endpoints
* **api:** add Update Bundle, which sets a Claude Tag Bundle's instructions, and return instructions on Bundle


### Bug Fixes

* **credentials:** write the credentials file on Windows with Python 3.12 and earlier
* **tools:** compare directory names exactly when confining file tool and upload paths on Windows
* **tools:** fully resolve file tool paths that pass through a dangling symlink
* **tools:** ignore ripgrep config files in the agent toolset's grep tool
* **tools:** keep an existing skill directory when the download or extraction that would replace it fails
* **tools:** keep the session tool runner's max_idle countdown running when a session thread terminates

  If the runner fails to read the session's event history after a reconnect, a termination that then arrives on the event stream still cancels the countdown, until the next idle or successful read.

* **tools:** leave symlinks that point outside /memories out of listings
* **tools:** look for ripgrep only in absolute `PATH` entries in the agent toolset's grep tool

  The tool no longer runs an `rg` from a relative or empty `PATH` entry or, on Windows, from the current directory. On Windows it looks for `rg.exe`, so an `rg.cmd`, `rg.bat` or `rg.com` is no longer used. With no other `rg` on `PATH`, the tool uses its built-in search.

* **tools:** pass over an rg inside the directories the agent toolset's file tools can write

  `grep` passes over an `rg` that resolves to somewhere inside `workdir` or `allowed_roots`, whatever the letter case of the names. It uses the next `rg` on `PATH`, or the built-in search when there is none. With a `workdir` that holds every `rg` on the host, such as `/`, every search is a built-in search. `rg` no longer gets the `ANTHROPIC_*` variables of the process, like the shell of `bash`.

* **tools:** read memory files only through the path that was validated
* **tools:** read only regular files in the grep tool's built-in search

  The built-in search of `grep` passes over a FIFO or a device in the directory it walks, as ripgrep does. Reading one could block the search, and the event loop with it, forever.

* **tools:** stop EnvironmentWorker from running tools for a terminated session

  For a terminated session, the worker now force-stops the work item right after it retrieves the session, before it downloads skills or memory stores. It no longer raises `SessionMemoryError` for such a session. The API reports an archived session as `terminated`.

* **tools:** stop the grep tool after 30 seconds of CPU time when ripgrep is not installed
* **tools:** stop the session tool runner from running the tool calls of a terminated session thread

  The runner also no longer yields these calls, including a denied call (`confirmation="deny"`) and a call to a tool that it does not own. The one exception is a call whose tool is already running when the thread terminates: the runner yields it with `posted=False` and posts no result.


### Chores

* **api:** deprecate old beta header values

  The API still accepts these values, but a later release removes them from the SDKs. Delete `prompt-caching-2024-07-31`, `pdfs-2024-09-25`, `token-counting-2024-11-01`, `token-efficient-tools-2025-02-19`, `extended-cache-ttl-2025-04-11`, `cache-diagnosis-2026-04-07` and `ce-user-management-2026-07-13` from your requests. `files-api-2025-04-14` and `skills-2025-10-02` select the beta response shapes, so follow the Files API and Skills migration guides before you delete them.

  In C#, the `AnthropicBeta` enum's members have new numbers, so code compiled against an earlier SDK version sends a different beta value, with no error, until you rebuild it.

* **api:** stop sending an old beta header on batch requests

  `beta.messages.batches` no longer sends `message-batches-2024-09-24`, which the API doesn't need. If your client sets a default `anthropic-beta` header, these requests now send it, where in some SDKs the old value replaced it. The API still accepts the old value. If you set it yourself, delete it: a later release removes it from the SDKs.

* **docs:** add an example value for the workspace name
* **docs:** clarify when the auto permission policy denies a tool call
* **docs:** clarify which workspaces an external key can be attached to
* **docs:** recommend multiagent_20261001 over the coordinator type
* **docs:** say when organization_id is required on plugin reads
* **tests:** let idle test workers take queued tests
